name: Nauru
summary: A single raised-coral island; its phosphate was mined by Germany, Britain, Australia and New Zealand, then by Nauru itself after independence in 1968. Briefly one of the richest countries, it was left with most of its land stripped.

location.value: Central Pacific near the equator; about 21 km².

terrain.value: A raised coral island with a mined-out plateau.

climate.value: Hot and humid equatorial climate, about 26–28 °C all year, with a wet monsoon season (November–February) and frequent droughts.

resources.value: Phosphate rock, formed from ancient seabird droppings and mined from 1906, now mostly exhausted; plus tuna in its waters.

disasters.value: Cyclones, droughts and rising sea levels.

population.value: About 12,000 people, most of them Nauruan, with other Pacific Islander, Chinese and other minorities.

urbanisation.value: There is no official capital; government offices are in Yaren district, and almost everyone lives on the narrow coastal strip around the island.

disease.value: Diabetes and heart disease from imported food.

migration.value: Some Nauruans move to Australia, New Zealand and Fiji for work and study; workers from Kiribati, Tuvalu and Asia came for the mines.

economicBase.value: Phosphate, fishing licences, Australian offshore detention centre.

tradeRoutes.value: Phosphate shipped to Australia and New Zealand from the cantilever loaders at Aiwo; Nauru Airlines flights link it to Brisbane and Pacific islands.

wealth.value: Briefly among the richest countries per person in the 1970s, then near bankruptcy by the 2000s after failed investments of phosphate money.

moneyAndTax.value: Uses the Australian dollar; government income comes mainly from fishing licences, the Australian-funded processing centre and aid.

inequality.value: Gap between the capital and outer islands.

governmentType.value: A parliamentary republic: Parliament (19 members) elects the president, who is both head of state and head of government.

keyRulers.value: Hammer DeRoburt, head chief before independence and first president (1968–76), who held several later terms until 1989.

succession.value: Presidents are elected by Parliament after general elections held at least every three years; no-confidence votes often change them.

institutions.value: A single-chamber Parliament, the president and cabinet, the Nauru Phosphate Royalties Trust and the Supreme Court.

stability.value: Frequent changes of government: in the 1990s–2000s presidents were often removed by no-confidence votes, sometimes several in a year.

eliteConflict.value: Rivalry among small groups of members of Parliament, often based on family and district ties rather than parties.

armyAndTech.value: Has no armed forces; a small police force keeps order, and Australia informally helps with defence.

territoryChange.value: No changes: the single island of about 21 km² has been its whole territory since independence.

alliancesRivals.value: Switched recognition from Taiwan to China (2024).

inventions.value: Traditional navigation by stars and swells.

scienceEducation.value: University of the South Pacific campuses.

openness.value: Open to outsiders and dependent on imports for almost all food, fuel and goods, shipped mainly from Australia.

communicationTransport.value: A single ring road around the island, Nauru International Airport with Nauru Airlines flights, and ships loading offshore.

religion.value: Mostly Christian: the Nauru Congregational Church is largest, followed by the Roman Catholic Church.

languageWriting.value: Nauruan, a Micronesian language spoken at home, and English, used in government and business.

artsArchitecture.value: Few historic buildings survive; traditions include string figures, frigatebird catching and dancing.

socialStructure.value: Twelve traditional clans (tribes), shown by the 12-pointed star on the flag; clan membership passes through the mother.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Nauruan identity based on clans, the Nauruan language and Angam Day (26 October), which marks the recovery of the population.

dailyLife.value: Most food is imported, such as rice and tinned meat; with little farmland, obesity and diabetes rates are among the highest in the world.

neighbours.value: No close neighbours: the nearest island is Banaba in Kiribati, about 300 km east; the Marshall Islands and Solomon Islands are farther off.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity and Pacific custom, plus debate over how to restore mined land and manage the trust funds left from phosphate.

riseSignals.value: Independence on 31 January 1968 after a campaign led by Hammer DeRoburt; Nauru took control of phosphate mining in 1970.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge, though the 1970s–1980s, when phosphate income was high, were its richest years.

declineSignals.value: Primary phosphate ran low by the 2000s and failed investments left the country near bankruptcy; it then relied on fishing licences and aid.

outcome.value: Still an independent republic and a member of the United Nations (since 1999) and the Commonwealth.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
